name: Ardor-Sabulum
specific_features: Surface glass created by orbital bombardment energy
Residual radiation signatures in specific zones
description: Ardor-Sabulum is a desert world whose surface tells a story of catastrophic violence, its sand seas interspersed with vast plains of glass created by energy releases sufficient to fuse the surface material to a depth of meters. The glass desert covers approximately thirty percent of the surface, its smooth expanses reflecting the sun with a blinding intensity that makes approach from certain angles impossible without optical protection. The fused sand formations at the margins of the glass zones rise in twisted, organic shapes where the heat gradient created partial melting, sand frozen mid-flow in sculptures of accidental beauty.

The thin atmosphere carries fine glass particles that make it hazardous to breathe and abrasive to exposed equipment, a persistent reminder of the violence that reshaped the surface. Thermal vent fields in the glass zones suggest that the energy that created them penetrated deep enough to affect subsurface geology, creating heat reservoirs that continue to warm the glass from below thousands of years after the event. The irradiated regolith zones coincide with the glass plains, confirming that the energy source was not natural volcanism but something far more concentrated and deliberate.

Analysis of the glass composition and radiation signatures points to directed energy weapons of extraordinary power, deployed from orbit against a surface that may once have been a conventional desert world. The pattern of strikes is systematic, covering the surface with overlapping zones of destruction that leave no area untouched, a sterilization protocol executed with methodical thoroughness. Dating methods place the event at approximately forty thousand years ago, consistent with the timeframe of destruction observed at Mortis-Silentium and Bellum-Crater.

The connection between Ardor-Sabulum and other destruction-dated worlds has intensified interest in identifying the responsible parties and understanding the scope of the conflict that produced such thorough devastation across multiple star systems. The fused silica glass has commercial value as an industrial material, and the rare earth elements concentrated by the bombardment energy are commercially extractable. But the planet's primary value is as evidence, a crime scene preserved in glass, radiation, and silence, its testimony waiting for investigators capable of reading the signatures of weapons that may one day be turned on worlds that still have something left to lose.
